standard.title: Turning Points of the Second World War — Holocaust and Atomic Bomb
standard.description: the significant events and turning points of the Second World War, including the Holocaust and use of the atomic bomb
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied significant events and turning points of World War One and their consequences, including the armistice and the human cost of industrialised warfare.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain why particular events were significant turning points in both theatres of the Second World War, investigate the Holocaust in historical context, and analyse the decision to use and the effects of the atomic bomb.

nodes.label: Turning points — European theatre
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why particular events were significant turning points in the European theatre of the Second World War.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why at least two events were turning points in the European theatre, identifying what changed as a result of each.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the significance of major European turning points: Germany's invasion of Poland (1939), the Blitzkrieg and fall of France, the Battle of Britain, Operation Barbarossa, the siege of Stalingrad, Operation Overlord (invasion of Normandy), the Battle of the Bulge, and the Soviets' capture of Berlin; for each, explain what made it a turning point (what shifted in terms of momentum, alliances, or strategic position).
wider: Examine the Eastern Front — Operation Barbarossa through to Stalingrad — as the theatre with the highest casualties and the decisive shift in German strategic capacity, comparing its scale with the Western Front narrative dominant in Australian curricula

Investigate Operation Overlord (D-Day) in depth as a case study in the complexity of military planning, examining the logistical, intelligence, and political dimensions alongside the military narrative

response_modes.reason: Students often describe events rather than analysing why they were turning points. Structure responses around the concept of 'turning point' explicitly — what shifted (momentum, resources, alliances, morale) — before asking students to apply the concept to specific events.

success_criteria: Identify at least two events as turning points in the European theatre and explain what specifically changed at each
Use the concept of 'turning point' correctly — distinguishing events that shifted the course of the war from those that were simply significant battles
Explain how momentum in the European theatre shifted between 1939 and 1945

nodes.label: Turning points — Asia-Pacific theatre
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why particular events were significant turning points in the Asia-Pacific theatre of the Second World War.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why at least two events were turning points in the Asia-Pacific theatre, including at least one that directly affected Australia.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the significance of major Asia-Pacific turning points: Japanese occupation of China, attack on Pearl Harbor (1941), fall of Singapore (1942), bombings of northern Australia, Battle of Midway (1942), Battle for Kokoda, Battle of Iwo Jima; explain the significance of each for the Allied war effort and for Australia specifically.
wider: Compare the significance of Pearl Harbor and the fall of Singapore as turning points — examining which more fundamentally changed the nature and scope of the Pacific War

Investigate the island-hopping campaign as a strategic turning point — examining how the Allied decision to bypass heavily defended islands and target strategic ones reshaped the final phase of the Pacific War

response_modes.reason: The Asia-Pacific theatre is often taught only through Australian-specific events. Including Pearl Harbor, the Battle of Midway, and the broader US strategic picture contextualises Australian events within the larger Allied campaign.

success_criteria: Identify at least two turning points in the Asia-Pacific theatre and explain their significance
Explain the strategic significance of the fall of Singapore for Australia's defence
Connect at least one Asia-Pacific turning point to a shift in the overall Allied strategic position

nodes.label: The Holocaust — context, scale, and significance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the Holocaust in its historical context, investigate its scale and significance using primary and secondary sources, and discuss its short- and long-term impacts.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the historical context in which the Holocaust occurred (anti-Semitism, Nazi race theory), describe its scale, and identify at least one short-term and one long-term impact on the Jewish community.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the historical context of the Holocaust including pre-existing anti-Semitism and Nazi race theory as ideology; investigate the scale and significance of the Holocaust using primary sources such as survivor testimonies and secondary sources; discuss short- and long-term impacts on the Jewish community — including coming to terms with the scale of loss, migration to Israel, Australia and the United States, and the creation of Yad Vashem and other Holocaust memorials.
wider: Examine a range of survivor testimonies alongside perpetrator accounts and bystander accounts, analysing how different positions of proximity to the Holocaust produce fundamentally different historical records

Investigate the long-term international legal legacy of the Holocaust — the Nuremberg Trials, the Genocide Convention (1948), and the concept of crimes against humanity — examining how the Holocaust reshaped international law

Explore the experiences of other persecuted groups during the Holocaust (Roma, disabled people, LGBTQI+ people, political prisoners) alongside the Jewish experience, examining what the targeting of multiple groups reveals about Nazi ideology
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who learn the Holocaust only as a list of facts — without understanding the ideology and social conditions that enabled it — are unable to engage meaningfully with the subsequent node on the atomic bomb decision or with K15 (origins of the UDHR), both of which depend on understanding how the Holocaust changed international moral frameworks.

response_modes.reason: Engage students in the historical question of how the Holocaust was possible — examining the role of ideology, bureaucracy, bystander complicity, and ordinary perpetrators — to move beyond description toward historical explanation.

Use survivor testimonies, perpetrator records, and bystander accounts as distinct source types — each revealing a different dimension of the Holocaust. This breadth of source type is essential for understanding how historians reconstruct events with incomplete and partial records.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Survivor testimony as a source type, the question of ordinary perpetrators, and the legal legacy of the Holocaust all offer rich analytical opportunities that extend beyond this descriptor into historical skills (S03, S04) and into the UDHR (K15).
success_criteria: Explain the historical context in which the Holocaust occurred, identifying anti-Semitism and Nazi race theory as enabling conditions
Describe the scale of the Holocaust and explain why survivor testimonies are significant as a source type for investigating it
Identify at least one short-term and one long-term impact of the Holocaust on the Jewish community

nodes.label: The atomic bomb — decision and effects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse why the atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and investigate their short- and long-term effects on human health and the environment.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain at least two reasons why the atomic bombs were dropped and describe at least one short-term and one long-term effect.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the race to build the atomic bomb (Germany, Japan, USA); analyse the reasons for dropping the bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki — military necessity, avoiding a land invasion, signalling to the Soviet Union, political pressure; investigate the short- and long-term effects on human health (blast, burns, radiation sickness, long-term cancer rates) and short- and long-term environmental effects on the cities and surrounding areas.
wider: Examine the competing historical interpretations of the decision to use the atomic bomb — 'military necessity' vs 'diplomatic signalling to the USSR' vs 'racism' arguments — evaluating which interpretation is best supported by available evidence

Compare the short- and long-term environmental and health legacies of Hiroshima and Nagasaki with later nuclear incidents (Chernobyl, Fukushima), examining how understanding of nuclear risk and responsibility has evolved

Investigate the Hibakusha (atomic bomb survivors) testimonies alongside US military and government records, examining how the same event is understood fundamentally differently depending on the standpoint of the source

response_modes.reason: The decision to drop the atomic bomb is a contested historical question with multiple interpretive frameworks. Explicitly teaching students to evaluate competing interpretations — rather than accepting the 'military necessity' narrative as given — builds the analytical skills required for K06, K20, and the S-strand.

The effects of the atomic bomb extend across human health, environmental damage, international law, and Cold War nuclear politics. Widening beyond the immediate blast effects to include long-term radiation health impacts and the nuclear arms race contextualises the bomb's significance.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The atomic bomb decision is a paradigm case for evaluating contested historical interpretations — a skill directly relevant to K20 (historical debates) and the S07 (analysing contested interpretations). The nuclear legacy also connects forward to K17 and K20.
success_criteria: Identify at least two reasons given for the decision to drop the atomic bombs and evaluate the strength of each reason
Describe the short- and long-term effects of the atomic bombs on human health
Explain why the use of atomic bombs is considered a turning point in both the Pacific War and in 20th-century history more broadly
